messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: your mail
parts:
> > The observer will be told what habitat he is being asked to sample in
> > the square and to go the centre of the 1 km square and find the nearest
> > piece of uniform habitat (>100mx100m). He is then to record the habitat
> > (using the BTO's BBS habitat recording codes). After allowing 5 minutes
> > for the birds to settle, the observer is to spend 10 minutes recording
> > each bird seen/heard within 4 bands: (0-10m; 10-25m; 25-100m; >100m).

There are a few problems with this methodology. Firstly, selecting the
nearest bit of uniform habitat negates the random design. It will for
example bias against species found mostly in mixed habitat. Far better
either to sample at the centre of each sampled square, and record habitat
category/categories within say 25m of the point, allowing you to
post-stratify analysis by habitat, or use your available data to stratify
by habitat in advance, and sample km squares from each habitat
classification. Also, counting for 10mins at each point will be
disastrous if you really want to estimate absolute numbers. Bird movement
will give you estimates of density an order of magnitude too high for some
species. Many surveys use this approach, and many of those have generated
very biased density estimates. The bias can be eliminated by doing a
'snapshot' count. Take a few minutes at the start, to determine what
birds are where, and of which species. Set your watch say to beep after
perhaps 5mins; that is your snapshot moment. Take a few more minutes to
confirm locations and identification of birds that were present at the
snapshot moment. If you really don't know where a bird was at that
moment, don't record a distance band for it - and exclude it from the
point transect analysis.

> > Having trialled the methodology over the past few days, I have the
> > following problems:
> >
> > 1. Much of Cumbria is farmland (50% or more). Many of the bird species
> > found in this habitat favour field edges such as hedges. Their
> > distribution is therefore not even. Anyone standing more than 100m from
> > the hedge will pick up the majority of the birds in the band (>
> > 100m). Similarly if one is right next to the hedge, the bulk of the
> > birds will be in the bands 0-10m and 10-25m. I personally cannot think
> > of a practical way around this. I suspect it also creates analytical
> > problems. Do you have any practical suggestions.

This is why it is critical that you do NOT instruct observers to locate a
patch of uniform habitat. The sample points should be random with respect
to the habitat, so the birds don't need to be. The problems you raise
then go away - points close to a hedge are balanced on average by points
further from a hedge, and distribution of birds, ON AVERAGE, is uniform
with respect to distance from a point in any given direction.

> > 2. Detectability. In the majority of passerine species, the male is
> > more obvious than the female during the breeding season.Should we be
> > recording different sexes where possible? Should we ignore females for
> > species where we can separate sexes? Does the program "Distance" allow a
> > correction?

For such species, analyse data for singing individuals. If you can assume
that this corresponds closely with adult males, and that there is roughly
one adult female per adult male, the (adult) abundance is then double your
estimate. If it makes more sense for a given species to record sex of
each individual, you can then stratify by sex, rather than by whether the
bird was singing. You can, in a separate analysis, estimate the
female/non-singing data, if you have sufficient data; that gives a check
of whether doubling your male estimate is reasonable.

> > 3. Analysis. We are planning two visits to each point - one in late
> > April/early May, the second late May/early June. Some resident species
> > are more detectable early on in the breeding season. In fact, I am aware
> > that in the space of a week, species like Marsh Tit can go from being
> > easy to count to difficult to find.
> >
> > Bearing this in mind, how should we proceed with the final analysis -
> > should we take the higher of the two counts as our estimate or should we
> > use both counts? I do not believe that the two counts are independant,
> > but would welcome some suggestions.

The higher of the 2 counts will again lead you to overestimate
abundance. For resident species that establish territory early, I would
use the early count only. For migrant species, I would use the late count
only. For intermediate species, I might analyse both the early counts and
the late counts in separate analyses, and if not significantly different,
perhaps average the two estimates, to give higher precision. This can be
done in Distance by stratifying the data by count date - early or late.

> > Banding - for an open habitat such as farmland, I suspect we may have
> > to lump together the habitat in the two closest bands and do a separate
> > analysis. For closed habitats such as woodland, the 10m band is likely
> > to have a reasonable number of birds in. In addition, visibility beyond
> > 25m is limited. Are we going to run into statstical problems if we lump
> > data together and do analyses for different habitats?

Lumping is not a problem, except that you are left with uncomfortably few
intervals for fitting and testing models. With 3 intervals, you can
either fit a one parameter model and have 1df left for testing model fit,
or fit a 2-parameter model, with no simple option for testing model fit.
I would have been inclined either to push your intervals out a bit - say
15m, 30m, 100m, or add at least one interval - say 10m, 25m, 75m, 150m. I
would also consider whether it is feasible to issue observers with
Bushnell binocs with laser rangefinders - in which case, allocation to
a larger number of intervals would be much easier. You should also
consider a training session with observers, to ensure that they can
estimate distance categories well.

Chris Sharpe on the Isle of Man is carrying out similar surveys as part of
their bird atlas, and has addressed many of these issues.

Steve Buckland
